top.label: Banks
top.blurb: Deposits, loans, and payments. Sized by balance sheet — what a bank holds, not what it manages for someone else.

sub.label: Sparkassen
sub.blurb: Public savings banks. Each city or county owns one. Retail deposits and local lending are the core business. 341 file annual accounts; our data covers a fraction of them.

sub.label: Landesbanken
sub.blurb: Wholesale banks owned by state governments and regional Sparkassen groups. They fund Sparkassen, lend to state-linked projects, and run capital-markets desks. Only 6 exist, and DekaBank is counted as one of them.

sub.label: Förder- und Zentralbanken
sub.blurb: State-owned development banks plus the cooperative sector's central bank. KfW is the largest. Bundesbank groups them together as banks with special, promotional and central support functions. 17 file annual accounts.

sub.label: Großbanken
sub.blurb: The three national full-service banks. Retail, corporate, and investment banking under one roof, nationwide branch networks. All three are in the data.

sub.label: Regionalbanken
sub.blurb: Everyone else with a German banking license: foreign banks' German subsidiaries, auto-finance banks, direct banks, and smaller private banks. A wide mix of sizes and models. 119 file annual accounts.

sub.label: Realkreditinstitute
sub.blurb: Mortgage banks. They fund long-term property loans, often through covered bonds (Pfandbriefe). A small, specialized group of 6.

sub.label: Bausparkassen
sub.blurb: Building societies. Customers save into a contract for years, then get a cheap home loan. A specific, regulated product line, not a general bank.

top.label: Asset Managers
top.blurb: Manage someone else's assets held on an outside balance sheet (often in a trust). The assets can be those of clients or could be assets held elsewhere in the corporate structure.

sub.label: Bank-owned
sub.blurb: Much of what they run is outside client money, because a bank's own book is loans and deposits rather than a managed portfolio.

views.subtitle: What financial institutions hold on their own balance sheets.
views.subtitle_2: One row per legal entity, on the same basis the official statistics count them, so the bars can be measured against a real sector total.

views.subtitle: What asset managers manage (on others' balance sheets).
views.subtitle_2: Not a second helping of the balance-sheet view. Much of this is money that also sits there, as some insurer's or bank's own investments.

views.subtitle: What corporate groups hold, counting each subsidiary once inside its parent.
views.subtitle_2: Munich Re is EUR 280bn here and EUR 111bn by sector. Both are right: German accounting carries a subsidiary at what the parent paid for it, however large it has since grown.

views.subtitle: What each group's asset managers run, grouped by who owns them.
views.subtitle_2: Deutsche Bank is the largest here because it owns DWS. The group holds none of this money itself.
